add_nodes.title: Debris tracked down to about 2 cm in the busiest shells
add_nodes.description: A shared, screening-grade catalog keeps custody of most objects larger than about 2 cm in the main constellation shells (450-600 km), several hundred thousand objects, with covariances good enough for conjunction screening. Operators can then screen against much of the 1-10 cm population that no catalog covers today.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: ESA's 2026 Space Environment Report counts about 1.2 million objects of 1-10 cm, nearly all untracked, against more than 40,000 catalogued objects. LeoLabs' sub-10 cm RANGER radar is in development. Space Fence (operational 2020, general) has not visibly grown the public catalog several-fold. Star trackers on constellations see roughly 10 cm and larger at useful ranges (general estimate).
add_nodes.pathway: P1 (association and orbit determination at 10^5-10^6 scale); sensor build-out and data sharing are not AI-math-driven
add_nodes.why: This is the second step on the sensor gate that limits LEO safety. Below about 3 cm, S-band radar returns fall roughly with the sixth power of object size (Rayleigh scattering, general), so cm-class custody needs higher-frequency or much larger radars and enough sites for daily revisit. AI applied math supplies the cognitive share: associating tracks and fitting orbits with honest covariances for several hundred thousand objects. Chain (S3): 5 cm catalog 2030 -> second-generation radars ordered 2030-31 and built 2031-33 -> association and covariance validation 2033 -> screening use 2034. S2 is a year later. S1 starts from its 2032 catalog and lands after 2035. Sensors compress about 1.0-1.3x and data sharing 1.0x, so S3 stays Low by 2035.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Radar power-aperture, money and willingness to share bind, and mathematics moves none of them. Operators can cut exposure to small debris by flying lower, where it decays within a few years, without tracking it at all.
add_nodes.signpost: A radar demonstrating custody of 2-3 cm objects in LEO (for example LeoLabs RANGER at full capability); a public or commercial catalog above 300,000 LEO objects with screening-grade covariances.
add_nodes.note_2035: Inside the horizon only in S2-S4, and only at the end of the window. S4 adds nothing because capital and data sharing bind the sensor build-out; robot construction crews would shorten site work by months at most.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-safe-orbits (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. New node for the 2035 horizon.

add_nodes.title: Debris removal becomes a recurring paid service
add_nodes.description: At least three defunct satellites or spent stages are removed in one calendar year, at least one of them paid under a commercial contract or a regulatory obligation. The servicers are built in series. Technology demonstrations do not count toward the three.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: No recurring removal service exists. ADRAS-J flew around an H-IIA upper stage at 15 m in 2024. ADRAS-J2 is planned for 2027, ClearSpace-1 for 2028 on Vega-C, and Astroscale's ELSA-M for Eutelsat, ESA and UKSA no earlier than 2028 (Wikipedia). All are first missions with government money behind them; who pays for routine removal is unresolved (general).
add_nodes.pathway: P7 (exogenous; AI math enters through safety-case and autonomy tools)
add_nodes.why: The first removal (2028 in every scenario) shows capture works. A recurring service also needs servicers built in series and a payer. Chain: first removals 2027-29 -> follow-on servicers ordered 2029-30 on the strength of those flights -> series production and launch 2031-33 -> three removals in one year about 2033. AI math trims each mission's test campaign and safety review through certified capture envelopes and assured autonomy. It creates no demand. Demand comes from disposal rules, liability, a capacity regime, or constellation operators removing their own failed satellites. Years and bands are the same in every scenario because payers and launches set the pace.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Removal may stay a handful of government demonstrations through 2035 because no one is obliged to pay. Dead satellites in lower shells reenter on their own within a few years.
add_nodes.signpost: ELSA-M results; a constellation operator or insurer paying to remove its own failed satellite; a government contract for several removals with one servicer design.
add_nodes.note_2035: A new 2035-horizon node. S4 gets no credit: ground robots could make servicers cheaper after 2031, but payers and launches bind, and budget-bound nodes get none.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-safe-orbits (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. New node for the 2035 horizon.

add_nodes.title: Chinese and Western constellations coordinate maneuvers automatically
add_nodes.description: At least one Western megaconstellation (for example Starlink) and at least one Chinese megaconstellation (Guowang or Qianfan) exchange ephemerides and maneuver intent machine to machine under an agreed protocol, and resolve close approaches without ad hoc human contact.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: No US-China ephemeris or maneuver-intent exchange exists. On Dec 9, 2025 a payload from a Chinese Kinetica-1 launch passed close to Starlink-6079 (reported about 200 m, unverified) with no coordination. Guowang and Qianfan are each planned above 10,000 satellites, and China filed for about 200,000 satellites at the ITU in Dec 2025.
add_nodes.pathway: P2 (verified protocol); the agreement itself is political
add_nodes.why: Chinese megaconstellations are the largest group of satellites outside Western coordination. Verified protocols (astro-coordination-protocols) and Western machine-to-machine coordination (astro-autonomous-ca-at-scale) make the technical bridge cheap. The gate is a government decision on both sides. Chain (S2): Western protocol operational 2031 -> technical talks and a pilot exchange 2032 -> agreed machine-readable exchange 2033 at the earliest. Politics runs at 1.0x in every scenario, so S3 and S4 match S2. S1 trails its 2033 Western rollout.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: US-China relations, export rules and military sensitivities may block any exchange whatever the math shows. Conjunction warnings already reach Chinese operators through existing channels (general), and both sides may judge that enough.
add_nodes.signpost: A published agreement between SpaceX and a Chinese operator, or between the US and Chinese governments, on ephemeris and maneuver-intent exchange; Chinese operators joining TraCSS or another shared screening service.

add_nodes.title: Storm arrival forecasts within about 6 hours using views from L5
add_nodes.description: The best routinely run CME arrival-time forecast reaches a mean absolute error of 6 h or less over at least 40 impacting CMEs, using real-time side-view coronagraph and heliospheric-imager data from ESA's Vigil, with calibrated probability windows.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: The best routinely run ensemble (Ensemble WSA-Enlil+Cone) has a mean absolute error of 10.3 h, and all CCMC scoreboard submissions together 13.2 h (Kay et al. 2024). Vigil carries NOAA's CCOR coronagraph, a heliospheric imager and a photospheric magnetic imager; it is planned to launch in Q3 2031 on Ariane 6, start quasi-nominal operations about 30 degrees from Earth and reach L5 after a cruise of about 3 years (Wikipedia).
add_nodes.why: Side views constrain CME speed and direction, which with the background solar wind dominate arrival error (Kay et al. 2024). With Vigil data from about 2033, assimilative ensembles built on the 8 h systems can run in real time. Validation runs on an event-count clock: with an error standard deviation near 15-17 h, about 40 impacting CMEs are needed, roughly two years as Cycle 26 rises. Chain (S2-S4): Vigil quasi-nominal data 2033 -> real-time ensembles with side-view imaging 2033 -> 40 events by 2035. The 6 h target is a judgment (illustrative). S1 reaches the 8 h step only in 2033 and lands after 2035.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Earlier side views from STEREO barely moved the error, and background solar-wind modeling may limit skill more than viewing angle. A one-year Vigil slip pushes the test beyond 2035.
add_nodes.signpost: Vigil launch on schedule (Q3 2031) and its first real-time heliospheric-imager products; a scoreboard model posting a mean absolute error below 7 h over 40 impacting CMEs.
add_nodes.note_2035: A new 2035-horizon node that lands only at the end of the window, in S2-S4. S4 adds nothing because launch and event-count clocks bind.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-safe-orbits (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. New node for the 2035 horizon.

add_nodes.title: Lunar navigation service with proven integrity in routine use
add_nodes.description: A lunar navigation service (ESA Moonlight, a LunaNet provider or a commercial relay) broadcasts with integrity monitoring whose protection levels carry machine-checked bounds, and at least three missions, including surface-base operations, use it as a primary navigation source.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: ESA Moonlight plans initial navigation services at end-2028, interoperability tests in 2029 and full operations in 2030; the Lunar Pathfinder relay is planned to begin operations in 2026 (ESA, Oct 2024). LuGRE obtained a GNSS fix on the lunar surface on Mar 3, 2025. NASA paused Gateway in its current form in Mar 2026 and redirected resources to a lunar surface base (NASA via 33FG). No lunar navigation service publishes integrity bounds yet.
add_nodes.why: Surface-base operations need navigation integrity like aviation GNSS has. Moonlight reaches full operations about 2030, and certified filters (2028 in S2) plus a flown monitor (2029) make an integrity-bounded service a software step. Chain (S2): flight demo 2029 -> integrity monitor in a provider's ground and user segments 2030-31 -> three missions using it as a primary source 2032. S3 cannot beat the lunar manifest, so it matches S2. S1 follows its 2031 demo by three years. Crewed use needs NASA or ESA acceptance, so 2035 is capped at Medium.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Accuracy is set by signals, clocks and geometry. Providers can publish integrity from conventional overbounding without machine-checked proofs, and missions may keep their own optical navigation as the primary source.
add_nodes.signpost: Moonlight or LunaNet service documents specifying formally verified protection levels; a lunar lander or surface-base operation naming the service as its primary navigation source.

patch.thesis: AI makes orbit, collision and space-weather forecasts honest. Certified million-object screening exists and AI-designed trajectories fly by 2029 (base case). Through 2035, safe low orbit waits on small-debris sensors, standards and US-China politics, and storm forecasts wait on Vigil from 2033. S4 adds nothing because no gate here is labor-bound.
patch.revision_note: B-safe-orbits: Thesis merges the advocate's two-curves framing (Stargaze) with the skeptic's increment point (HASDM, Stargaze shrink the AI-math share); trajectory flight year 2028 -> 2029 and screening dated 2029 (skeptic). Reader hook: auditor's corrections (about 330x, rounded to 'about 300 times'; 13.2 h is the all-submission average, best ensemble 10.3 h). Spine: astro-small-debris-catalog inserted before LEO safety as its binding gate. | C-fix (2026-10-07): spine rebuilt so it forms one connected chain of hard edges that reaches tier 6-7. Trunk nodes ['cap-research-math-public', 'cap-applied-math'] are shown as the chain's entry anchors (also listed in roots); they stay members of the trunk branch only. No spine nodes dropped. | E-safe-orbits (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. Thesis rewritten for 2026-2035 and S4; reader hook kept. Spine extended by astro-35-cross-bloc-coordination (hard edge from astro-autonomous-ca-at-scale) and astro-35-cm-debris-custody (hard edge from astro-small-debris-catalog).

notes: E-safe-orbits: all 31 branch nodes reviewed for 2035 and S4; every legacy '>2031' resolved (19 scenario-years). S4 equals S3 in every node, by year and by band, because the branch's gates are cognitive, data, adoption, formalization, regulatory, capital and launch gates; the S4 analysis puts every one of its tier 5-7 nodes in no_move, and none passes the four-condition rule after 2032. band_2035 rises where four more years remove timing doubt (S1 cognition reaches the S2 2029-30 level by 2035) and stays put where nature, sensors, classification or politics bind (eruption onset, Bz, missile-tracking attribution). Vigil (launch Q3 2031, quasi-nominal operations about 2033, L5 about 2034) resolves the side-view monitor to 2033 in every scenario. Five new nodes extend chains into 2032-35: cm-class debris custody and cross-bloc maneuver coordination (spine), a recurring paid removal service, L5-based storm arrival forecasts and a lunar navigation service with proven integrity. All new ids use the astro-35- prefix; the storm forecast node keeps domain 'plasma'. Robot soft edges (in-space assembly and aerospace tolerance work to the removal service, construction trades to cm-class custody) are accelerators only and earn no S4 credit.
